links.note: Kievan Rus' took its Christian books and its letters from the Cyril and Methodius mission. Mouravieff, a Russian church historian writing in 1838, says the brothers' Slavonic Bible later helped win the Russians to the faith. Herberstein retold the Rus' annals in 1549. He says the Rus' began to write down their past once the Slavonic letters came.

Sigmund von Herberstein, Notes upon Russia (Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentarii, 1549), trans. R. H. Major (1851), vol. I: a sixteenth-century retelling of the Rus' annals, used here as a later account, not as a primary for the ninth century: the Rus' annals 'began to be written and recorded' after Michael 'had sent the Sclavonian characters into Bulgaria' (which the same passage dates [898])

All support is now nineteenth-century or earlier secondary (Mouravieff 1838, Pinkerton 1814, Herberstein 1549), which is the open question on Dominant Modern Reconstruction resting on old secondaries (escalation 10).

He says Russia has kept the faith of Christ since Vladimir's baptism.

links.note: In the 850s a church law of the patriarch Theodosius told the far-off metropolitans, India's among them, to write to him every six years. A Malabar manuscript of 1301 names Jacob, metropolitan of 'the holy see of the Apostle St. Thomas'. At Kollam in the fourteenth century, the papal envoy Marignolli found the pepper gardens owned by 'the Christians of St. Thomas'. Few texts survive from the centuries between, so the line rests on place, name and office.

links.note: Peter of Sicily, a Byzantine envoy at Tephrike around 870, wrote that the Paulicians meant to send preachers to Bulgaria. Older historians, and some modern ones, built a line from them to the Bogomils on reports like this. Others point out that the Armenian sources show no dualism, and doubt the line. No Paulician or Bogomil text settles it.

links.note: The see of Skara in Sweden dates from Sigfrid, the missionary who baptized King Olof Skötkonung, the historian Anjou writes. Its bishop left in 1529. The cathedral's provost, Sven, was chosen in his place, and a church council at Uppsala backed him in 1530. Denmark broke harder. In 1536 the bishops in Copenhagen were jailed, and the church law of 1537 set a superintendent over each diocese instead. This rests on one history from the 1850s, with four centuries between the two ends, so the line is thin.

prose_changes.old: These conversions became the national churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, which have existed continuously ever since. The Jelling stones still stand in Denmark, hundreds of Christian rune stones survive across Sweden, and St Olaf's shrine at Nidaros made Trondheim the great pilgrimage destination of the medieval north. Iceland's later saga writers also preserved the memory of the conversion in the words of the converted rather than of the missionaries.
prose_changes.new: These conversions founded what became the national churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland. In Sweden the Reformation often kept the old sees and cathedrals and reformed them. Denmark broke more sharply. In 1536 it jailed its bishops and handed their work to new men. The period left a physical record too. The Jelling stones still stand in Denmark, and hundreds of Christian rune stones survive across Sweden. St Olaf's shrine at Nidaros made Trondheim the great goal of pilgrims in the medieval north. Iceland's later saga writers also kept the memory of the conversion. They told it in the words of the converted, not of the missionaries.

prose_changes.old: Only a small community at Toledo kept the name into modern times. Mozarabic Christianity was worn away from two sides. Almoravid and Almohad rule pressed hard on it, and the Latin church of the northern kingdoms took it in as they advanced. Its liturgy, though, outlived the people who kept it. The Mozarabs held on to the old Hispanic rite when the rest of the Latin West took up Roman usage. Around 1500 Cardinal Cisneros rescued it at Toledo. He had its books printed and endowed a chapel to keep it in use. Mass in the Hispano-Mozarabic rite is still said there every day.

prose_changes.old: The movement continued in the Balkans for centuries — its story runs on directly into the Bogomil communities of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries — before disappearing under Ottoman rule and Catholic and Orthodox pressure alike. Its most discussed legacy is a claimed influence on the Cathars of southern France and northern Italy. Medieval writers asserted the connection, and historians still argue about how much of it is real. What it did not leave is a text of its own. Every surviving account of Bogomil belief was written by someone opposing it.

What it did not leave is a text of its own. Every account of Bogomil belief that survives was written by someone who opposed it.
